source: Here, we demonstrate that AVP neuron activity is regulated by multiple anatomically and functionally distinct neural circuits.

claim: Presystemic regulation during drinking is mediated by circuits involving the lamina terminalis.
source: Notably, presystemic regulation during drinking and eating are mediated by non-overlapping circuits that involve the lamina terminalis and hypothalamic arcuate nucleus, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Presystemic regulation during eating is mediated by circuits involving the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus.
source: Notably, presystemic regulation during drinking and eating are mediated by non-overlapping circuits that involve the lamina terminalis and hypothalamic arcuate nucleus, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Presystemic regulation during drinking and eating are mediated by non-overlapping circuits.
source: Notably, presystemic regulation during drinking and eating are mediated by non-overlapping circuits that involve the lamina terminalis and hypothalamic arcuate nucleus, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Rapid, anticipatory feedforward regulation is a common feature of many homeostatic circuits.
source: Rapid, anticipatory feedforward regulation is a common feature of many homeostatic circuits (Betley et al., 2015; Zimmerman et al., 2016; Augustine et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Feedforward regulation plays an important role in shaping ingestive behavior by promoting negative-reinforcement learning.
source: Several studies have shown that feedforward regulation plays an important role in shaping ingestive behavior by promoting negative-reinforcement learning (Betley et al., 2015; Allen et al., 2017; Leib et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Feedforward regulation is crucial for maintaining energy/water balance as it prevents overconsumption by preemptively terminating ingestive behavior before systemic disturbance is detected.
source: It is also suggested that feedforward regulation is crucial for maintaining energy/water balance as it prevents overconsumption by preemptively terminating ingestive behavior before systemic disturbance is detected (Andermann and Lowell, 2017; Augustine et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The idea of feedforward regulation in the hypothalamus existed since the late 1900s.
source: Although the significance of feedforward regulation is just beginning to be recognized, the idea of such regulation in the hypothalamus existed since the late 1900s.
evidence: This is a historical statement about the field.

claim: Studies looking at the effect of water intake on thirst and blood vasopressin (AVP) levels provided a conceptual framework for feedforward regulation.
source: A conceptual framework for feedforward regulation was provided by studies looking at the effect of water intake on thirst and blood vasopressin (AVP) levels (Rolls et al., 1980; Wood et al., 1980; Thrasher et al., 1981; Stricker and Hoffmann, 2007), from which the term 'presystemic regulation' originates.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The term 'presystemic regulation' originates from studies looking at the effect of water intake on thirst and blood vasopressin levels.
source: A conceptual framework for feedforward regulation was provided by studies looking at the effect of water intake on thirst and blood vasopressin (AVP) levels (Rolls et al., 1980; Wood et al., 1980; Thrasher et al., 1981; Stricker and Hoffmann, 2007), from which the term 'presystemic regulation' originates.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: AVP is also known as antidiuretic hormone.
source: AVP, also known as antidiuretic hormone, is synthesized by posterior pituitary-projecting magnocellular AVP neurons of the paraventricular (PVH) and supraoptic nuclei (SON) of the hypothalamus.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: AVP is synthesized by posterior pituitary-projecting magnocellular AVP neurons of the paraventricular (PVH) and supraoptic nuclei (SON) of the hypothalamus.
source: AVP, also known as antidiuretic hormone, is synthesized by posterior pituitary-projecting magnocellular AVP neurons of the paraventricular (PVH) and supraoptic nuclei (SON) of the hypothalamus.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Magnocellular AVP neurons underlie the body's main non-behavioral response to dehydration or elevated systemic osmolality—an increase in circulating AVP.
source: These neurons underlie the body's main non-behavioral response to dehydration or elevated systemic osmolality—an increase in circulating AVP.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Upon stimulation of AVP neurons, AVP is released from the axon terminals in the posterior pituitary and enters the bloodstream.
source: Upon stimulation of AVP neurons, AVP is released from the axon terminals in the posterior pituitary and enters the bloodstream (Ferguson et al., 2003; Bolignano et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Once released, AVP binds to receptors in the kidney and stimulates water reabsorption to restore water balance.
source: Once released, AVP binds to receptors in the kidney and stimulates water reabsorption to restore water balance (Nielsen et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Activity of AVP neurons is regulated by two temporally distinct mechanisms.
source: Activity of AVP neurons is regulated by two temporally distinct mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Feedback or systemic regulation mainly informs AVP neurons of changes in systemic water balance.
source: Feedback or systemic regulation, which mainly informs AVP neurons of changes in systemic water balance, is mediated by the lamina terminalis (LT), comprised of the subfornical organ (SFO), median preoptic nucleus (MnPO), and organum vasculosum lamina terminalis (OVLT) (McKinley et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Feedback or systemic regulation is mediated by the lamina terminalis (LT), comprised of the subfornical organ (SFO), median preoptic nucleus (MnPO), and organum vasculosum lamina terminalis (OVLT).
source: Feedback or systemic regulation, which mainly informs AVP neurons of changes in systemic water balance, is mediated by the lamina terminalis (LT), comprised of the subfornical organ (SFO), median preoptic nucleus (MnPO), and organum vasculosum lamina terminalis (OVLT) (McKinley et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The SFO and OVLT are circumventricular organs (CVOs) that lack a blood-brain barrier.
source: The SFO and OVLT are circumventricular organs (CVOs) that lack a blood-brain barrier, and are capable of sensing systemic osmolality and blood-borne factors, such as angiotensin II.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The SFO and OVLT are capable of sensing systemic osmolality and blood-borne factors, such as angiotensin II.
source: The SFO and OVLT are circumventricular organs (CVOs) that lack a blood-brain barrier, and are capable of sensing systemic osmolality and blood-borne factors, such as angiotensin II.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Osmolality information sensed by the SFO and OVLT is sent to AVP neurons directly or indirectly via the MnPO.
source: Osmolality information sensed by the SFO and OVLT is then sent to AVP neurons directly or indirectly via the MnPO.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Feedforward or presystemic regulation informs AVP neurons of anticipated future osmotic perturbation, based on the array of presystemic signals that occur immediately before (pre-ingestive) and after (post-ingestive) food or water ingestion.
source: Feedforward or presystemic regulation, on the other hand, informs AVP neurons of anticipated future osmotic perturbation, based on the array of presystemic signals that occur immediately before (pre-ingestive) and after (post-ingestive) food or water ingestion (Stricker and Hoffmann, 2007; Stricker and Stricker, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Presystemic regulation of AVP release was first described in 1980, in a study using dehydrated dogs.
source: Presystemic regulation of AVP release was first described in 1980, in a study using dehydrated dogs (Thrasher et al., 1981; Thrasher et al., 1987), and was later replicated in humans, monkeys, sheep, and rats (Arnauld and du Pont, 1982; Geelen et al., 1984; Blair-West et al., 1985; Huang et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Presystemic regulation of AVP release was later replicated in humans, monkeys, sheep, and rats.
source: Presystemic regulation of AVP release was first described in 1980, in a study using dehydrated dogs (Thrasher et al., 1981; Thrasher et al., 1987), and was later replicated in humans, monkeys, sheep, and rats (Arnauld and du Pont, 1982; Geelen et al., 1984; Blair-West et al., 1985; Huang et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Studies demonstrated that drinking causes a rapid reduction in blood AVP levels and that this decrease precedes any detectable decrease in blood osmolality (i.e., it is presystemic).
source: These studies demonstrated that drinking causes a rapid reduction in blood AVP levels and that this decrease precedes any detectable decrease in blood osmolality (i.e., it is presystemic).
evidence: This statement refers to findings from previously cited studies.

claim: Due to lack of temporal resolution in blood AVP measurements, previous studies failed to capture rapid dynamics of presystemic regulation.
source: However, due to lack of temporal resolution in blood AVP measurements (Christ-Crain and Fenske, 2016), these studies failed to capture rapid dynamics of presystemic regulation, preventing further dissection of distinct stimuli causing the presystemic reductions in AVP.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In a previous study, magnocellular AVP neurons were demonstrated to be under bidirectional presystemic regulation by drinking and eating.
source: In a previous study, we demonstrated that magnocellular AVP neurons are under bidirectional presystemic regulation by drinking and eating (Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The neural inputs providing presystemic information to AVP neurons are still unclear.
source: However, the neural inputs providing presystemic information to these neurons are still unclear.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Magnocellular SONAVP and PVHAVP neurons receive strong inputs from the SFO, MnPO, and OVLT.
source: Remarkably, despite their distinctly different anatomical locations, but in agreement with their identical functions, rabies mapping results from magnocellular PVHAVP and SONAVP neurons were strikingly similar. Both received strong inputs from the SFO, MnPO, and OVLT (Figure 1d and h), and additional sparse rabies labeling was found in the arcuate nucleus (ARC) of the hypothalamus and the perinuclear zone (PNZ), an area surrounding the SON.
evidence: This finding is based on rabies mapping data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Rabies mapping results from magnocellular PVHAVP and SONAVP neurons were strikingly similar.
source: Remarkably, despite their distinctly different anatomical locations, but in agreement with their identical functions, rabies mapping results from magnocellular PVHAVP and SONAVP neurons were strikingly similar.
evidence: This is an observation from the rabies mapping experiments.

claim: Additional sparse rabies labeling was found in the arcuate nucleus (ARC) of the hypothalamus and the perinuclear zone (PNZ) in rabies mapping from SONAVP and PVHAVP neurons.
source: Both received strong inputs from the SFO, MnPO, and OVLT (Figure 1d and h), and additional sparse rabies labeling was found in the arcuate nucleus (ARC) of the hypothalamus and the perinuclear zone (PNZ), an area surrounding the SON.
evidence: This finding is based on rabies mapping data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Dense rabies labeling was found in the PVH when inputs to SONAVP neurons were examined.
source: We also found surprisingly dense rabies labeling in the PVH and SON when inputs to SONAVP and PVHAVP neurons were examined, respectively (Figure 1c and g).
evidence: This finding is based on rabies mapping data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Dense rabies labeling was found in the SON when inputs to PVHAVP neurons were examined.
source: We also found surprisingly dense rabies labeling in the PVH and SON when inputs to SONAVP and PVHAVP neurons were examined, respectively (Figure 1c and g).
evidence: This finding is based on rabies mapping data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Neurons in the PVH do not send direct projections to the SON.
source: First, we injected AAV that Cre-independently expresses ChR2-mCherry into either the PVH or SON and found that neurons in these sites do not send direct projections to the SON and PVH, respectively.
evidence: This finding is based on anterograde tracing experiments.

claim: Neurons in the SON do not send direct projections to the PVH.
source: First, we injected AAV that Cre-independently expresses ChR2-mCherry into either the PVH or SON and found that neurons in these sites do not send direct projections to the SON and PVH, respectively.
evidence: This finding is based on anterograde tracing experiments.

claim: Axosomatic and axodendritic PVH → SONAVP or SON → PVHAVP connections do not exist.
source: Based on these results, we believe that axosomatic and axodendritic PVH → SONAVP or SON → PVHAVP connections do not exist, and we speculate that the above-mentioned rabies results were caused by either non-synaptic transfer of rabies (i.e., an artifact) or synaptic transfer via axoaxonic synapses that might exist between PVH and SON neurons at the level of the posterior pituitary (Silverman et al., 1983; Choudhury and Ray, 1990).
evidence: This conclusion is based on anterograde and retrograde tracing experiments, and is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The rabies labeling in PVH and SON was caused by either non-synaptic transfer of rabies or synaptic transfer via axoaxonic synapses that might exist between PVH and SON neurons at the level of the posterior pituitary.
source: Based on these results, we believe that axosomatic and axodendritic PVH → SONAVP or SON → PVHAVP connections do not exist, and we speculate that the above-mentioned rabies results were caused by either non-synaptic transfer of rabies (i.e., an artifact) or synaptic transfer via axoaxonic synapses that might exist between PVH and SON neurons at the level of the posterior pituitary (Silverman et al., 1983; Choudhury and Ray, 1990).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the rabies mapping results, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The MnPO/OVLT sends both excitatory and inhibitory projections to the PVH and SON.
source: We found that the MnPO/OVLT sends both excitatory and inhibitory projections to the PVH and SON while the SFO only sends excitatory projections (Figure 1j).
evidence: This finding is based on anterograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: The SFO only sends excitatory projections to the PVH and SON.
source: We found that the MnPO/OVLT sends both excitatory and inhibitory projections to the PVH and SON while the SFO only sends excitatory projections (Figure 1j).
evidence: This finding is based on anterograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Lack of long-range inhibitory projections of the SFO has been previously reported.
source: Lack of long-range inhibitory projections of the SFO has been previously reported (Oka et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: SFOVglut2 and MnPO/OVLTVglut2 neurons provided robust glutamatergic input to PVHAVP and SONAVP neurons.
source: We found that SFOVglut2 and MnPO/OVLTVglut2 neurons provided robust glutamatergic input to PVHAVP and SONAVP neurons (Figure 1l and n).
evidence: This finding is based on CRACM experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: GABAergic input from MnPO/OVLTVgat neurons was detected only in half of the PVHAVP and SONAVP neurons.
source: In contrast, GABAergic input from MnPO/OVLTVgat neurons was detected only in half of the PVHAVP and SONAVP neurons.
evidence: This finding is based on CRACM experiments.

claim: The MnPO/OVLT provided glutamatergic and GABAergic input to the majority of GFP-negative neurons in the PVH and SON.
source: The MnPO/OVLT provided glutamatergic and GABAergic input to the majority of GFP-negative neurons in the PVH and SON.
evidence: This finding is based on CRACM experiments.

claim: SFO Vglut2 neurons do not provide direct synaptic input to GFP-negative PVH neurons.
source: We did not find any connection between SFO Vglut2 neurons and GFP-negative PVH neurons, suggesting that SFO Vglut2 inputs were highly specific to AVP neurons.
evidence: This finding is based on CRACM experiments.

claim: SFO Vglut2 inputs were highly specific to AVP neurons.
source: We did not find any connection between SFO Vglut2 neurons and GFP-negative PVH neurons, suggesting that SFO Vglut2 inputs were highly specific to AVP neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on CRACM experiments.

claim: PVHAVP and SONAVP neurons receive excitatory and inhibitory inputs from the LT.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that PVHAVP and SONAVP neurons receive excitatory and inhibitory inputs from the LT.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the circuit mapping experiments.

claim: Inhibition of the MnPO/OVLT abolished the pre-ingestive drop in SONAVP neuron activity in response to water bowl placement.
source: Inhibition of the MnPO/OVLT abolished the pre-ingestive drop in SONAVP neuron activity (Figure 2b–f).
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments with chemogenetic inhibition shown in Figure 2.

claim: Inhibition of the MnPO/OVLT significantly attenuated the post-ingestive response of SONAVP neurons.
source: The post-ingestive response was also significantly attenuated.
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments with chemogenetic inhibition.

claim: The pre-ingestive response of SONAVP neurons was learning-dependent as it gradually developed over the course of training.
source: This pre-ingestive response was learning-dependent as it gradually developed over the course of training (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is based on data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pre- and post-ingestive suppression of SONAVP neurons were observed before the significant drop in systemic osmolality.
source: Pre- and post-ingestive suppression of SONAVP neurons were observed before the significant drop in systemic osmolality, which we previously found to begin 10–15 min after drinking onset (Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: MnPO/OVLT inhibition did not prevent drinking but delayed drinking onset as demonstrated by a significant increase in the latency to drink.
source: MnPO/OVLT inhibition did not prevent drinking but delayed drinking onset as demonstrated by a significant increase in the latency to drink (Figure 2g).
evidence: This finding is based on behavioral data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The number of drinking bouts per session was not affected by MnPO/OVLT inhibition.
source: The number of drinking bouts per session was not affected.
evidence: This finding is based on behavioral data.

claim: The MnPO/OVLT, along with the SFO, is the main source of excitatory input that underlies activation of SONAVP neurons during systemic hyperosmolality.
source: The MnPO/OVLT, along with the SFO, is the main source of excitatory input that underlies activation of SONAVP neurons during systemic hyperosmolality (McKinley et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: MnPO/OVLT inhibition caused a drop in the baseline activity of SONAVP neurons in water-restricted mice.
source: Consistent with this, we found that MnPO/OVLT inhibition caused a drop in the baseline activity of SONAVP neurons in water-restricted mice (Figure 2h).
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments with chemogenetic inhibition shown in Figure 2.

claim: Inhibition of the SFO caused a slight but non-significant attenuation of pre- and post-ingestive suppression of SONAVP neurons.
source: Inhibition of the SFO caused a slight but non-significant attenuation of pre- and post-ingestive suppression (Figure 2j–l).
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments with chemogenetic inhibition shown in Figure 2.

claim: Neurons in the MnPO/OVLT are important mediators of water-related presystemic signals to AVP neurons.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that neurons in the MnPO/OVLT are important mediators of water-related presystemic signals to AVP neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the chemogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: SON-projecting MnPO/OVLTVglut2 neurons received inputs from multiple sites including the SFO, PVH, VMH, DMH, and LPBN.
source: Results from the MnPO/OVLT and SFO were strikingly different. SON-projecting MnPO/OVLTVglut2 neurons received inputs from multiple sites (Figure 3c), including the SFO, PVH, ventromedial (VMH), and dorsomedial nuclei (DMH) of the hypothalamus, and the lateral parabrachial nucleus (LPBN).
evidence: This finding is based on rabies mapping data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Among the inputs to SON-projecting MnPO/OVLTVglut2 neurons, the SFO contained the greatest number of rabies-labeled neurons.
source: Among these areas, the SFO contained the greatest number of rabies-labeled neurons, demonstrating strong interconnectivity between these LT structures.
evidence: This finding is based on rabies mapping data.

claim: SON-projecting SFOVglut2 neurons received inputs only from the other LT structures, the MnPO and OVLT.
source: In contrast, SON-projecting SFOVglut2 neurons received inputs only from the other LT structures, the MnPO and OVLT (Figure 3f).
evidence: This finding is based on rabies mapping data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The MnPO/OVLT is the primary LT region that receives and relays extra-LT inputs to AVP neurons.
source: These data suggest that the MnPO/OVLT is the primary LT region that receives and relays extra-LT inputs to AVP neurons and, thus, is likely the main entry point for water-related presystemic information.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rabies mapping data.

claim: The MnPO/OVLT is likely the main entry point for water-related presystemic information.
source: These data suggest that the MnPO/OVLT is the primary LT region that receives and relays extra-LT inputs to AVP neurons and, thus, is likely the main entry point for water-related presystemic information.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rabies mapping data.

claim: Rabies-labeled collateral projections of SON-projecting MnPO/OVLTVglut2, MnPO/OVLTVgat, and SFOVglut2 neurons were found in the PVH and LT.
source: We found rabies-labeled collateral projections of SON-projecting MnPO/OVLTVglut2, MnPO/OVLTVgat, and SFOVglut2 neurons in the PVH and LT (Figure 3g–i).
evidence: This finding is based on rabies-based axon collateral mapping shown in Figure 3.

claim: The density of collateral projections was lower than that of the projections to the SON, suggesting that only a subset of SON-projecting MnPO/OVLTVglut2, MnPO/OVLTVgat, and SFOVglut2 neurons send collaterals to the PVH and LT.
source: The density of collateral projections was lower than that of the projections to the SON, suggesting that only a subset of SON-projecting MnPO/OVLTVglut2, MnPO/OVLTVgat, and SFOVglut2 neurons send collaterals to the PVH and LT.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rabies-based axon collateral mapping data.

claim: MnPO/OVLT-projecting SFOVglut2 neurons send a similar density of rabies-labeled fibers to the MnPO/OVLT, PVH, and SON.
source: Interestingly, we found that MnPO/OVLT-projecting SFOVglut2 neurons, which include thirst-promoting neurons (Matsuda et al., 2017; Augustine et al., 2018), send a similar density of rabies-labeled fibers to the MnPO/OVLT, PVH, and SON (Figure 3j).
evidence: This finding is based on rabies-based axon collateral mapping shown in Figure 3.

claim: A majority of SON-projecting SFOVglut2 neurons send collaterals to the MnPO/OVLT and PVH.
source: This result suggests that a majority of these SON-projecting SFOVglut2 neurons send collaterals to the MnPO/OVLT and PVH, and, therefore may be capable of simultaneously regulating AVP release and thirst.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rabies-based axon collateral mapping data.

claim: SON-projecting SFOVglut2 neurons may be capable of simultaneously regulating AVP release and thirst.
source: This result suggests that a majority of these SON-projecting SFOVglut2 neurons send collaterals to the MnPO/OVLT and PVH, and, therefore may be capable of simultaneously regulating AVP release and thirst.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the rabies-based axon collateral mapping data.

claim: Downstream projections of the LT are redundantly organized such that presystemic information is shared between the LT structures and between PVHAVP and SONAVP neurons via collateral projections.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that, unlike convergence of afferent presystemic inputs to the MnPO/OVLT, downstream projections of the LT are redundantly organized such that presystemic information is shared not only between the LT structures but also between PVHAVP and SONAVP neurons via collateral projections.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the collateral mapping experiments.

claim: SON-projecting MnPO/OVLTVglut2 and SFOVglut2 neurons both showed an immediate drop in activity upon water bowl placement.
source: We found that SON-projecting MnPO/OVLTVglut2 and SFOVglut2 neurons both showed an immediate drop in activity upon water bowl placement (Figure 4b–e).
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: A further drop in activity of SON-projecting MnPO/OVLTVglut2 and SFOVglut2 neurons was observed as drinking continued.
source: A further drop in activity was observed as drinking continued.
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments.

claim: The response of SON-projecting MnPO/OVLTVglut2 and SFOVglut2 neurons resembled the response of SONAVP neurons.
source: This resembled the response of SONAVP neurons, suggesting that the inputs from MnPO/OVLTVglut2 and SFOVglut2 neurons contribute to water-related presystemic regulation of AVP neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fiber photometry data.

claim: The inputs from MnPO/OVLTVglut2 and SFOVglut2 neurons contribute to water-related presystemic regulation of AVP neurons.
source: This resembled the response of SONAVP neurons, suggesting that the inputs from MnPO/OVLTVglut2 and SFOVglut2 neurons contribute to water-related presystemic regulation of AVP neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fiber photometry data.

claim: MnPO/OVLTVglut2 neurons showed a larger and sharper decrease in activity compared to SFOVglut2 neurons when normalized values were compared.
source: MnPO/OVLTVglut2 neurons showed a larger and sharper decrease in activity compared to SFOVglut2 neurons when normalized values were compared (Figure 4f).
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Activity of MnPO/OVLTVglut2 neurons reached <50% of baseline activity within the first 1 min of drinking.
source: Activity of MnPO/OVLTVglut2 neurons reached <50% of baseline activity within the first 1 min of drinking, whereas SFOVglut2 neurons showed a gradual decrease that continued for over 5 min.
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments.

claim: SFOVglut2 neurons showed a gradual decrease in activity that continued for over 5 min during drinking.
source: Activity of MnPO/OVLTVglut2 neurons reached <50% of baseline activity within the first 1 min of drinking, whereas SFOVglut2 neurons showed a gradual decrease that continued for over 5 min.
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments.

claim: A sharper drop in MnPO/OVLTVglut2 neuron activity is consistent with significant attenuation of water-related presystemic response by MnPO, but not SFO, inhibition.
source: A sharper drop in MnPO/OVLTVglut2 neuron activity is consistent with significant attenuation of water-related presystemic response by MnPO, but not SFO, inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the fiber photometry data with the chemogenetic inhibition results.

claim: SON-projecting MnPO/OVLTVgat neurons showed an abrupt increase in activity upon placement of the water bowl.
source: Placement of the water bowl caused an abrupt increase in MnPO/OVLTVgat neuron activity, which rapidly declined and returned to baseline within 1 min.
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments.

claim: The activity of SON-projecting MnPO/OVLTVgat neurons rapidly declined and returned to baseline within 1 min after water bowl placement.
source: Placement of the water bowl caused an abrupt increase in MnPO/OVLTVgat neuron activity, which rapidly declined and returned to baseline within 1 min.
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments.

claim: No drinking-related, long-term responses were observed in SON-projecting MnPO/OVLTVgat neurons.
source: No drinking-related, long-term responses were observed.
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments.

claim: SON-projecting MnPO/OVLTVgat neurons mainly signal the anticipation of water and work in parallel with MnPO/OVLTVglut2 and SFOVglut2 neurons to ensure rapid inhibition of AVP neuron activity upon water bowl placement.
source: We hypothesize that SON-projecting MnPO/OVLTVgat neurons mainly signal the anticipation of water and work in parallel with MnPO/OVLTVglut2 and SFOVglut2 neurons to ensure rapid inhibition of AVP neuron activity upon water bowl placement.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the fiber photometry data.

claim: The MnPO/OVLT is a key relay center for water-related presystemic information.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that the MnPO/OVLT is a key relay center for water-related presystemic information.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the fiber photometry experiments.

claim: Inhibition of MnPO/OVLTVglut2 neurons caused an overall reduction of water-related presystemic responses in SONAVP neurons.
source: Inhibition of MnPO/OVLTVglut2 neurons caused an overall reduction of water-related presystemic responses in SONAVP neurons. Both pre- and post-ingestive responses were significantly affected (Figure 5b–f).
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments with chemogenetic inhibition shown in Figure 5.

claim: Inhibition of MnPO/OVLTVglut2 neurons significantly affected both pre- and post-ingestive responses of SONAVP neurons.
source: Inhibition of MnPO/OVLTVglut2 neurons caused an overall reduction of water-related presystemic responses in SONAVP neurons. Both pre- and post-ingestive responses were significantly affected (Figure 5b–f).
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments with chemogenetic inhibition shown in Figure 5.

claim: Inhibition of excitatory neurons in the MnPO/OVLT was less effective in reducing pre-ingestive component of the response compared to non-specific silencing of the same area, as ~30% of the pre-ingestive response persisted.
source: However, in comparison to non-specific silencing of the same area, which caused a complete removal of the pre-ingestive response of SONAVP neurons (Figure 2f), inhibition of excitatory neurons in the MnPO/OVLT was less effective in reducing pre-ingestive component of the response as ~30% of the pre-ingestive response persisted (Figure 5g).
evidence: This is a comparison of results from different chemogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: MnPO/OVLTVglut2 neuron inhibition caused a significant reduction in the amount of water intake.
source: However, when mice were tested in a separate setup using a lickometer, MnPO/OVLTVglut2 neuron inhibition caused a significant reduction in the amount of water intake in the same group of animals (Figure 5h).
evidence: This finding is based on behavioral data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The effect of MnPO/OVLTVgat neuron inhibition was strictly restricted to the pre-ingestive phase.
source: In contrast, the effect of MnPO/OVLTVgat neuron inhibition was strictly restricted to the pre-ingestive phase (Figure 5k–o).
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments with chemogenetic inhibition shown in Figure 5.

claim: A significant reduction in the SONAVP neuron response was found only during the last 5 s of pre-ingestive period that immediately precedes the onset of drinking when MnPO/OVLTVgat neurons were inhibited.
source: More specifically, a significant reduction in the SONAVP neuron response was found only during the last 5 s of pre-ingestive period that immediately precedes the onset of drinking (Figure 5p).
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments with chemogenetic inhibition shown in Figure 5.

claim: Water-predicting cue/pre-ingestive information is primarily conveyed by inhibitory neurons of the MnPO/OVLT.
source: The degree of reduction in pre-ingestive responses (Figure 5p) was comparable to that of non-specific silencing of the MnPO/OVLT (Figure 2f), suggesting that water-predicting cue/pre-ingestive information is primarily conveyed by inhibitory neurons of the MnPO/OVLT.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of chemogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: Inhibition of MnPO/OVLTVgat neurons had no effect on post-ingestive responses or baseline activity of SONAVP neurons.
source: Consistent with a lack of post-ingestive or any sustained changes in the activity of MnPO/OVLTVgat neurons in response to drinking (Figure 4h–k), their inhibition had no effect on post-ingestive responses or baseline activity of SONAVP neurons (Figure 5p and r).
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments with chemogenetic inhibition shown in Figure 5.

claim: Drinking behavior was not altered by MnPO/OVLTVgat neuron inhibition during the experimental session or when tested in a separate setup.
source: Drinking behavior was not altered during the experimental session or when tested in a separate setup (Figure 5q).
evidence: This finding is based on behavioral data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Excitatory and inhibitory inputs from the MnPO/OVLT are each responsible for pre- and post-ingestive drops in SONAVP neuron activity, respectively.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that excitatory and inhibitory inputs from the MnPO/OVLT are each responsible for pre- and post-ingestive drops in SONAVP neuron activity, respectively, and that both inputs are required for water-related presystemic responses of SONAVP neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the chemogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: Both excitatory and inhibitory inputs from the MnPO/OVLT are required for water-related presystemic responses of SONAVP neurons.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that excitatory and inhibitory inputs from the MnPO/OVLT are each responsible for pre- and post-ingestive drops in SONAVP neuron activity, respectively, and that both inputs are required for water-related presystemic responses of SONAVP neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the chemogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: MnPO/OVLT inhibition did not affect the baseline activity or feeding-induced activation of SONAVP neurons.
source: MnPO/OVLT inhibition did not affect the baseline activity (not shown) or feeding-induced activation (Figure 6a–c).
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments with chemogenetic inhibition shown in Figure 6.

claim: Food-related presystemic regulation is mediated by a different circuit that does not involve the MnPO/OVLT.
source: These results demonstrate that food-related presystemic regulation is mediated by a different circuit that does not involve the MnPO/OVLT.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the chemogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: None of the SON-projecting LT neurons displayed responses that could account for feeding-induced activation observed in SONAVP neurons.
source: In line with the result from MnPO/OVLT inhibition, none of the SON-projecting LT neurons displayed responses that could account for feeding-induced activation observed in SONAVP neurons (Figure 6d and e).
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: SON-projecting SFOVglut2 and MnPO/OVLTVglut2 neurons showed an overall decrease in activity after food presentation but no consistent pattern was observed.
source: SON-projecting SFOVglut2 and MnPO/OVLTVglut2 neurons showed an overall decrease in activity after food presentation but no consistent pattern was observed.
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments.

claim: SON-projecting MnPO/OVLTVgat neurons were activated by food presentation but their activity gradually declined following feeding onset.
source: SON-projecting MnPO/OVLTVgat neurons were activated by food presentation but their activity gradually declined following feeding onset.
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments.

claim: The amplitude of food-related responses in SON-projecting MnPO/OVLTVgat neurons was significantly smaller than water-related responses of the same neurons.
source: The amplitude of these responses was significantly smaller than water-related responses of the same neurons (Figure 6e).
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Presystemic activation of SONAVP neurons is time-locked to the feeding onset.
source: Presystemic activation of SONAVP neurons is time-locked to the feeding onset (this study and Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in the current study and a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: SON-projecting SFOVglut2, MnPO/OVLTVglut2, and MnPO/OVLTVgat neurons all showed a decrease in activity when traces were aligned to feeding onset.
source: SON-projecting SFOVglut2, MnPO/OVLTVglut2, and MnPO/OVLTVgat neurons all showed a decrease in activity (Figure 6f).
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: A small, simultaneous decrease in excitatory and inhibitory tone is unlikely to be the primary cause of rapid feeding-induced activation of SONAVP neurons.
source: Even if these were to be bona fide responses, a small, simultaneous decrease in excitatory and inhibitory tone is unlikely to be the primary cause of rapid feeding-induced activation of SONAVP neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fiber photometry data.

claim: A previous study demonstrated rapid net activation of all excitatory SFO neurons by food intake.
source: A previous study demonstrated rapid net activation of all excitatory SFO neurons by food intake (Zimmerman et al., 2016), which contradicts our finding.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Blood osmolality begins to gradually increase as early as within 1-2 min of feeding and reaches significance at 5 min.
source: Given that blood osmolality begins to gradually increase as early as within 1-2 min of feeding and reaches significance at 5 min (Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2017), we speculate that feeding-induced activation of SFOVglut2 neurons reflects systemic blood osmolality changes.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Feeding-induced activation of SFOVglut2 neurons reflects systemic blood osmolality changes.
source: Given that blood osmolality begins to gradually increase as early as within 1-2 min of feeding and reaches significance at 5 min (Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2017), we speculate that feeding-induced activation of SFOVglut2 neurons reflects systemic blood osmolality changes.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the fiber photometry data and previous findings.

claim: MnPO/OVLT and SFO are not involved in presystemic feeding-induced activation of SONAVP neurons.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that MnPO/OVLT and SFO are not involved in presystemic feeding-induced activation of SONAVP neurons, supporting our finding that food- and water-related presystemic regulation is mediated by non-overlapping neural circuits.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the fiber photometry experiments.

claim: Food- and water-related presystemic regulation is mediated by non-overlapping neural circuits.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that MnPO/OVLT and SFO are not involved in presystemic feeding-induced activation of SONAVP neurons, supporting our finding that food- and water-related presystemic regulation is mediated by non-overlapping neural circuits.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the fiber photometry experiments.

claim: Projections from the NTS were extremely sparse in the PVH and nearly absent in the SON.
source: Projections from the NTS were extremely sparse in the PVH and nearly absent in the SON (Figure 7a).
evidence: This finding is based on anterograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: The NTS does not provide direct synaptic input to AVP neurons.
source: Subsequent CRACM showed that the NTS do not provide direct synaptic input to AVP neurons (Figure 7b and c).
evidence: This finding is based on CRACM experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: A1/C1 neurons are crucial for hypotension-induced AVP release.
source: A1/C1 neurons are suggested to be crucial for hypotension-induced AVP release as non-specific inhibition/lesion of the VLM causes a significant attenuation of this response (Blessing and Willoughby, 1985; Head et al., 1987).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A1/C1 inhibition significantly attenuated the activation of SONAVP neurons in response to drug-induced hypotension.
source: A1/C1 inhibition significantly attenuated the activation of SONAVP neurons in response to drug-induced hypotension (Figure 7e).
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments with chemogenetic inhibition shown in Figure 7.

claim: A1/C1 neuron inhibition had no effect on feeding-induced activation of SONAVP neurons.
source: In contrast to the robust blockade of hypotension-induced SONAVP neuron activation, A1/C1 neuron inhibition had no effect on feeding-induced activation of SONAVP neurons (Figure 7f).
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments with chemogenetic inhibition shown in Figure 7.

claim: Blood pressure regulation is mediated by a circuit involving A1/C1 neurons and this circuit is distinct from the food-related presystemic circuit.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that blood pressure regulation is mediated by a circuit involving A1/C1 neurons and this circuit is distinct from the food-related presystemic circuit.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the chemogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: AgRP and POMC projections were present in the PVH and SON but no synaptic connections were detected between AgRP/POMC and AVP neurons.
source: AgRP and POMC projections were present in the PVH and SON but no synaptic connections were detected between AgRP/POMC and AVP neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This finding is based on projection mapping and CRACM experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Specific chemogenetic inhibition of AgRP or POMC neurons had no effect on the food-related presystemic response of SONAVP neurons.
source: In line with this, specific chemogenetic inhibition of AgRP or POMC neurons had no effect on the food-related presystemic response of SONAVP neurons when investigated using fiber photometry in AVP-IRES-Cre;AgRP/POMC-IRES-Cre mice (Figure 7h–j).
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments with chemogenetic inhibition shown in Figure 7.

claim: Short-term (<30 min following CNO injection) feeding behavior was not altered by AgRP or POMC neuron inhibition.
source: Short-term (<30 min following CNO injection) feeding behavior was not altered by AgRP or POMC neuron inhibition (Figure 7—figure supplement 4 and Krashes et al., 2011; Üner et al., 2019).
evidence: This finding is based on behavioral data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4 and is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: GABAergic neurons in the PNZ (PNZVgat) are believed to be involved in hypertension- and hypervolemia-induced inhibition of SONAVP neurons.
source: GABAergic neurons in the PNZ (PNZVgat) are believed to be involved in hypertension- and hypervolemia-induced inhibition of SONAVP neurons (Grindstaff and Cunningham, 2001b; Grindstaff and Cunningham, 2001a; Cunningham et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PNZVgat neurons provided direct inhibitory input to AVP neurons.
source: While we found that PNZVgat neurons provided direct inhibitory input to AVP neurons and showed a selective response to food but not water (Figure 7—figure supplement 2b, f), inhibition of these neurons had no effect on the baseline activity of SONAVP neurons (not shown) or their response to feeding (Figure 7—figure supplement 2g,i).
evidence: This finding is based on CRACM and fiber photometry experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: PNZVgat neurons showed a selective response to food but not water.
source: While we found that PNZVgat neurons provided direct inhibitory input to AVP neurons and showed a selective response to food but not water (Figure 7—figure supplement 2b, f), inhibition of these neurons had no effect on the baseline activity of SONAVP neurons (not shown) or their response to feeding (Figure 7—figure supplement 2g,i).
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Inhibition of PNZVgat neurons had no effect on the baseline activity of SONAVP neurons or their response to feeding.
source: While we found that PNZVgat neurons provided direct inhibitory input to AVP neurons and showed a selective response to food but not water (Figure 7—figure supplement 2b, f), inhibition of these neurons had no effect on the baseline activity of SONAVP neurons (not shown) or their response to feeding (Figure 7—figure supplement 2g,i).
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments with chemogenetic inhibition shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: AgRP, POMC, and PNZVgat neurons are not primary contributors to food-related presystemic regulation.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that AgRP, POMC, and PNZVgat neurons are not primary contributors to food-related presystemic regulation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the circuit mapping and chemogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: Inhibition of neurons in all three nuclei (ARC+VMH+DMH) caused a significant attenuation of feeding-induced activation that persisted throughout the recording.
source: Inhibition of neurons in all three nuclei (ARC+VMH+DMH) caused a significant attenuation of feeding-induced activation that persisted throughout the recording (Figure 7l–n).
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments with chemogenetic inhibition shown in Figure 7.

claim: Inhibition of the VMH alone, fully sparing the ARC, had no effect on feeding-induced activation of SONAVP neurons.
source: In contrast, inhibition of the VMH (Figure 7p) or DMH (Figure 7r) alone, fully sparing the ARC, had no effect.
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments with chemogenetic inhibition shown in Figure 7.

claim: Inhibition of the DMH alone, fully sparing the ARC, had no effect on feeding-induced activation of SONAVP neurons.
source: In contrast, inhibition of the VMH (Figure 7p) or DMH (Figure 7r) alone, fully sparing the ARC, had no effect.
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry experiments with chemogenetic inhibition shown in Figure 7.

claim: Injection of CNO in all three groups (ARC+VMH+DMH, VMH only, DMH only) did not affect the baseline activity of SONAVP neurons or short-term feeding behavior of mice.
source: Injection of CNO in all three groups did not affect the baseline activity of SONAVP neurons (not shown) or short-term feeding behavior of mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This finding is based on fiber photometry and behavioral experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: The ARC contains a cell type, distinct from AgRP or POMC neurons, that relay food-related presystemic signals to SONAVP neurons.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the ARC contains a cell type, distinct from AgRP or POMC neurons, that relay food-related presystemic signals to SONAVP neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the chemogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: AVP neuron activity, and thus likely AVP release, is altered surprisingly rapidly by water and food ingestion before any change in systemic osmolality is observed.
source: In a prior study, by directly monitoring the activity of magnocellular AVP neurons, we demonstrated that AVP neuron activity, and thus likely AVP release, is altered surprisingly rapidly by water and food ingestion before any change in systemic osmolality is observed (Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: AVP neurons are unique in that they are capable of responding presystemically to both water and food.
source: While such feedforward, presystemic regulation has been demonstrated in other homeostatic circuits, AVP neurons are unique in that they are capable of responding presystemically to both water and food, and the response is bidirectional—water-predicting cues and drinking inhibit and eating activates AVP neurons—and asymmetric—water causes pre- and post-ingestive presystemic inhibition but food only causes post-ingestive presystemic activation.
evidence: This is a statement about the unique properties of AVP neurons based on previous findings.

claim: The response of AVP neurons to water and food is bidirectional—water-predicting cues and drinking inhibit and eating activates AVP neurons.
source: While such feedforward, presystemic regulation has been demonstrated in other homeostatic circuits, AVP neurons are unique in that they are capable of responding presystemically to both water and food, and the response is bidirectional—water-predicting cues and drinking inhibit and eating activates AVP neurons—and asymmetric—water causes pre- and post-ingestive presystemic inhibition but food only causes post-ingestive presystemic activation.
evidence: This is a statement about the unique properties of AVP neurons based on previous findings.

claim: The response of AVP neurons to water and food is asymmetric—water causes pre- and post-ingestive presystemic inhibition but food only causes post-ingestive presystemic activation.
source: While such feedforward, presystemic regulation has been demonstrated in other homeostatic circuits, AVP neurons are unique in that they are capable of responding presystemically to both water and food, and the response is bidirectional—water-predicting cues and drinking inhibit and eating activates AVP neurons—and asymmetric—water causes pre- and post-ingestive presystemic inhibition but food only causes post-ingestive presystemic activation.
evidence: This is a statement about the unique properties of AVP neurons based on previous findings.

claim: The study revealed two parallel, non-overlapping neural pathways for water- and food-related presystemic regulation.
source: Our study revealed two parallel, non-overlapping neural pathways for water- and food-related presystemic regulation (Figure 8, Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study summarized in the discussion.

claim: Key components of the water-related presystemic circuit are neurons in the LT, which provide direct synaptic input to AVP neurons and exhibit water-related presystemic responses that closely resemble those of AVP neurons.
source: Key components of the water-related presystemic circuit are neurons in the LT, which provide direct synaptic input to AVP neurons and exhibit water-related presystemic responses that closely resemble those of AVP neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study.

claim: Food-related presystemic regulation is mediated by an as yet unidentified neuronal population in the ARC that is completely distinct from feeding-regulating AgRP and POMC neurons.
source: Food-related presystemic regulation, on the other hand, is mediated by an as yet unidentified neuronal population in the ARC that is completely distinct from feeding-regulating AgRP and POMC neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study.

claim: Water- versus food-related presystemic signals are relayed to AVP neurons independently and differently via two non-overlapping circuits to give rise to the bidirectional, asymmetric presystemic response of AVP neurons.
source: Collectively, these findings demonstrate that water- versus food-related presystemic signals are relayed to AVP neurons independently and differently via two non-overlapping circuits to give rise to the bidirectional, asymmetric presystemic response of AVP neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: Recent studies have identified multiple molecularly or anatomically distinct neuronal populations in the LT that are involved in different aspects of water homeostasis.
source: Recent studies have identified multiple molecularly or anatomically distinct neuronal populations in the LT that are involved in different aspects of water homeostasis ( Abbott et al., 2016; Allen et al., 2017; Matsuda et al., 2017; Augustine et al., 2018; Matsuda et al., 2020; Pool et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: At least three groups of LT neurons provide direct input to AVP neurons: SFOVglut2, MnPO/OVLTVglut2, and MnPO/OVLTVgat neurons.
source: We identified at least three groups of LT neurons that provide direct input to AVP neurons: SFOVglut2, MnPO/OVLTVglut2, and MnPO/OVLTVgat neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study.

claim: While all three groups of LT neurons (SFOVglut2, MnPO/OVLTVglut2, and MnPO/OVLTVgat) connect to AVP neurons with high probability, only MnPO/OVLT neurons were required for their presystemic regulation.
source: Interestingly, while all these neurons connect to AVP neurons with high probability, only MnPO/OVLT neurons were required for their presystemic regulation.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study.

claim: MnPO/OVLT neurons played no role in mediating food-related presystemic responses.
source: More strikingly, while being indispensable for water-related presystemic responses of AVP neurons, MnPO/OVLT neurons played no role in mediating food-related presystemic responses, indicating that presystemic regulation of AVP neurons involves two distinct neural pathways dedicated to water- or food-related regulation.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study.

claim: Presystemic regulation of AVP neurons involves two distinct neural pathways dedicated to water- or food-related regulation.
source: More strikingly, while being indispensable for water-related presystemic responses of AVP neurons, MnPO/OVLT neurons played no role in mediating food-related presystemic responses, indicating that presystemic regulation of AVP neurons involves two distinct neural pathways dedicated to water- or food-related regulation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: Presystemic responses of thirst-regulating counterparts of the LT have been extensively studied by many groups.
source: Presystemic responses of thirst-regulating counterparts of the LT have been extensively studied by many groups (Zimmerman et al., 2016; Allen et al., 2017; Augustine et al., 2018; Augustine et al., 2019; Zimmerman et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Thirst-regulating LT neurons exhibit presystemic suppression (thirst-promoting neurons) and activation (thirst-suppressing neurons).
source: While thirst-regulating LT neurons also exhibit presystemic suppression (thirst-promoting neurons) and activation (thirst-suppressing neurons), their responses surprisingly lack a pre-ingestive component that is present in AVP-regulating LT neurons and also hunger-regulating AgRP and POMC neurons (this study and Betley et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Thirst-regulating LT neuron responses lack a pre-ingestive component that is present in AVP-regulating LT neurons and also hunger-regulating AgRP and POMC neurons.
source: While thirst-regulating LT neurons also exhibit presystemic suppression (thirst-promoting neurons) and activation (thirst-suppressing neurons), their responses surprisingly lack a pre-ingestive component that is present in AVP-regulating LT neurons and also hunger-regulating AgRP and POMC neurons (this study and Betley et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies and data from the current study.

claim: The MnPO is traditionally considered as a hub that functions as the main input and output region of the LT.
source: The MnPO is traditionally considered as a hub that functions as the main input and output region of the LT (McKinley et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Magnocellular PVHAVP and SONAVP neurons, despite their distinct anatomical locations, are functionally identical.
source: Magnocellular PVHAVP and SONAVP neurons, despite their distinct anatomical locations, are functionally identical, receive inputs from the same sites (Figure 1), and show similar presystemic responses (Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by data from the current study and a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Magnocellular PVHAVP and SONAVP neurons receive inputs from the same sites.
source: Magnocellular PVHAVP and SONAVP neurons, despite their distinct anatomical locations, are functionally identical, receive inputs from the same sites (Figure 1), and show similar presystemic responses (Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by data from the current study shown in Figure 1.

claim: Magnocellular PVHAVP and SONAVP neurons show similar presystemic responses.
source: Magnocellular PVHAVP and SONAVP neurons, despite their distinct anatomical locations, are functionally identical, receive inputs from the same sites (Figure 1), and show similar presystemic responses (Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Systemic osmolality information (from the CVOs [the SFO and OVLT]) and water-related presystemic information (from yet-undefined regions outside the LT) converge on the MnPO/OVLT.
source: Systemic osmolality information (from the CVOs [the SFO and OVLT]) and water-related presystemic information (from yet-undefined regions outside the LT) converge on the MnPO/OVLT and are redistributed to AVP neurons and other downstream targets directly, or indirectly via the SFO.
evidence: This is an inference based on the circuit mapping data.

claim: Information converging on the MnPO/OVLT is redistributed to AVP neurons and other downstream targets directly, or indirectly via the SFO.
source: Systemic osmolality information (from the CVOs [the SFO and OVLT]) and water-related presystemic information (from yet-undefined regions outside the LT) converge on the MnPO/OVLT and are redistributed to AVP neurons and other downstream targets directly, or indirectly via the SFO.
evidence: This is an inference based on the circuit mapping data.

claim: The DMH is known to play a role in presystemic regulation of AgRP neurons.
source: The DMH is of particular interest as it is already known to play a role in presystemic regulation of AgRP neurons (Garfield et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The LPBN is known to relay interoceptive information to forebrain sites.
source: The LPBN is also of interest in that it is known to relay interoceptive information to forebrain sites (Herbert et al., 1990), and it has been strongly implicated in regulation of water balance (Davern, 2014; Gizowski and Bourque, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The LPBN has been strongly implicated in regulation of water balance.
source: The LPBN is also of interest in that it is known to relay interoceptive information to forebrain sites (Herbert et al., 1990), and it has been strongly implicated in regulation of water balance (Davern, 2014; Gizowski and Bourque, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Recent studies identified two groups of thirst-suppressing neurons in the PBN that send direct projections to the MnPO/OVLT and exhibit post-ingestive activation in response to drinking.
source: Indeed, recent studies identified two groups of thirst-suppressing neurons in the PBN that send direct projections to the MnPO/OVLT and exhibit post-ingestive activation in response to drinking (Ryan et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Many anatomical and electrophysiological studies have demonstrated that AVP neurons receive direct excitatory and inhibitory projections from the ARC.
source: Many anatomical and electrophysiological studies have demonstrated that AVP neurons receive direct excitatory and inhibitory projections from the ARC (Iijima and Ogawa, 1981; Saphier and Feldman, 1986; Leng et al., 1988; Ludwig and Leng, 2000; Pineda et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Oxytocin receptor-expressing glutamatergic neurons are a good candidate for mediating food-related presystemic regulation as these neurons are activated by feeding and are capable of inhibiting food intake rapidly when activated.
source: Oxytocin receptor-expressing glutamatergic neurons (Fenselau et al., 2017) are a good candidate for mediating food-related presystemic regulation as these neurons are activated by feeding and are capable of inhibiting food intake rapidly when activated.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion based on a citation to a previous study.

claim: Convergence and integration of multiple inputs at the level of AVP neurons, the final common pathway for AVP release, provide a neural circuit basis for differential regulation of AVP release by diverse behavioral and physiological stimuli.
source: Convergence and integration of multiple inputs at the level of AVP neurons, the final common pathway for AVP release, provide a neural circuit basis for differential regulation of AVP release by diverse behavioral and physiological stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.
